Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn As more Romanian families weigh international education options, the IB Diploma Programme stands out for combining academic breadth with independent research and critical thinking. Romania Insider spoke with Doria Draghiciu, Deputy Head of Secondary High School at Verita International School in Bucharest, about how the IB's inquiry-based approach differs from traditional education, how universities view the diploma, and the school's recent highlights, including its strongest IB results in recent years, with a cohort average of 32.2 points and one student scoring 44 out of 45. How does the IB's inquiry-based approach differ from more traditional models of education? Doria Draghiciu: The IB inquiry-based approach differs from more traditional models of education mainly in the way knowledge is constructed and used. In a traditional model, knowledge is transferred from the teacher to the student directly. The student uses it to solve some kind of exercise and is then assessed on whether they can reproduce that knowledge on a test. The IB does not reject knowledge taken in this way or direct instruction. In fact, strong inquiry cannot happen without subject knowledge. Where the IB differs is that it asks students to go beyond the acquisition of knowledge. Students are challenged to question, make connections, investigate and build models in unfamiliar situations, as well as reflect on the process of learning itself. In order to do this, the process starts from the practical experience and builds the abstract concepts afterwards. Students start with an applied example and find the general rules after identifying the patterns. In this sense, the role of the teacher is central and shifts from the traditional model. The teacher is still an expert and provides knowledge, explanation, feedback, and assessment, but the lessons are transformed into learning experiences that require students to be conceptual learners and independent thinkers. The goal is not only for students to acquire knowledge, but that they look at what they know with more flexibility, judgement, and intellectual curiosity. How do universities weigh the IB Diploma against A-Levels, AP, or national curricula in admissions decisions? Doria Draghiciu: Universities recognise the IB Diploma as a strong and challenging qualification, alongside A Levels, AP, and national curricula. Each system has its own strengths. A Levels allow students to specialise earlier, and AP offers flexibility, especially for students applying within the American system. At Verita, one of the reasons we value the IB Diploma is that it gives students both breadth and depth. Students study six subjects , so they continue to develop across languages, humanities, sciences, mathematics, and the arts or electives, while also going deeper in their Higher Level subjects. This means they do not close doors too early, but they still have the academic depth needed for competitive university courses. Through its Diploma Core , the IB also gives universities a fuller picture of the student. Through the Extended Essay (EE), students complete independent research. Through the Theory of Knowledge (TOK), they learn to question how knowledge is built and evaluated. Through Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS), they engage with creativity, activity, and service beyond the classroom. So universities are not only seeing subject grades, but also evidence of research skills, critical thinking, time management, reflection, and balance. I would not frame the IB as better than every other system for every student. But I do think its advantage is that it prepares students very well for university life, not only because of what they study, but because of how they learn to think, manage work, and take responsibility for their own learning. How does Verita support students in their IBDP? Doria Draghiciu: At Verita, we support students in the IB DP through both academic and pastoral structures. Students have strong subject teaching, but they are also supported through Core time, TOK, CAS, Extended Essay guidance, mock exams, reflection meetings, academic tracking, university counselling, and individual follow-up. The DP is not only challenging because of the content. It is challenging because students have to manage deadlines, independent research, internal assessments, exams, CAS, and university planning at the same time. So our role is to help students understand the programme, plan ahead, and build the habits they need to manage it well. We also work closely as a team. Teachers, the DP Coordinator, the counsellor, learning support, parents, and students themselves are all part of the support system. Our aim is to help students become independent, but not isolated. They are expected to take ownership, but we give them the structures and guidance to learn how to do that. How do you involve parents in their child's DP journey? Doria Draghiciu: We involve parents by trying to make the Diploma Programme less mysterious. From the outside, the DP can look like just another school programme with final exams at the end, but it is much more layered than that. There are internal assessments, the Extended Essay, TOK, CAS, predicted grades, university applications, and deadlines that come at different moments across the two-year programme. So our role is to communicate clearly and early on, not only when something has gone wrong. We use parent information sessions , individual meetings, reports, emails, and follow-up conversations to help parents understand both the programme and their child's progress. I think parents are an important part of the DP journey, but their role is not to manage things for the student. Their role is to understand the pressure points, support routines at home, encourage balance, and help students become more independent over time. What were the school's highlights in the past academic year? Doria Draghiciu: The Class of 2026 delivered Verita's strongest IB Diploma results in recent years, marking the highest cohort average of 32.2 points. One student's near-perfect score of 44 out of a possible 45 points stands out as an exceptional achievement, placing them among the very top IB performers worldwide. One of the main highlights of the past academic year was our IB evaluation visit. It was an important moment for Verita because it allowed us to pause, reflect on the Diploma Programme, and look honestly at both our strengths and our next steps. The process confirmed many things we are proud of, especially our culture of care , our student support, and the way teachers work together around students. We also continued to strengthen the Core of the programme, especially TOK, CAS, and the Extended Essay. The TOK Exhibition was a real highlight this year. It was a hit with students, teachers, and the wider school community, and it gave students a meaningful opportunity to show how they are thinking about knowledge, perspective, evidence, and real-world objects. Another important highlight was the development of our university counselling programme, supported by the Dukes network, which has significantly improved the way we support students in thinking about pathways, careers, and university choices. This has made the process more intentional and has helped students and families have these conversations earlier and with more clarity. For me, the highlight is not a single event. It is seeing the programme become more intentional, more coherent, and more connected to who we are as a school. *This business view wast edited by Romania Insider for Verita. https://www.indcatholicnews.com/news/556.text: Home News UK & Ireland US & Canada World Obituaries & Tributes Justice, Peace & Environment Education Youth & Young Adults Reflections Reflections & Homilies Viewpoint Letters Blogs Arts & Culture Gospel in Art Art, Theatre, Music & Shows Films, TV & Radio Books Poetry Travel Listings Forthcoming Events Regular Events Classified Ads Jobs Courses & Voluntary Work Retreat, Spirituality and Pilgrimage Centres Businesses, Accommodation & Travel Prayers Contact Resources Links About Cardinal Wiseman students celebrate results Two schools in Coventry and Birmingham are celebrating a stellar set of A-level and Level 3 vocational results. Cardinal Wiseman Catholic School - Coventry This school, part of the Romero Catholic Academy, has reported improvement in the number of students achieving the highest grades, with many securing places at leading universities and highly competitive degree apprenticeships. Students will now progress to Russell Group universities, other leading universities, degree apprenticeships and employment. Harryson Barber achieved A, A, A in mathematics, physics and chemistry. He said: "I got the grades I needed to do what I wanted to do, so I'm really pleased and ready to start the next stage of my life. "I'm now going to start a degree apprenticeship in civil engineering with Jacobs. I wasn't as keen on the traditional university route, and the apprenticeship will give me a job while helping me to develop the skills I need for my future career. "I've always enjoyed a challenge, which is why I chose these A-levels, and I'm really pleased that all the hard work has paid off." Kacper Ciepinski achieved A, B, A, A in mathematics, further mathematics, Polish and physics. He said: "I was pretty nervous to open my results. I'm now going to study mechanical engineering at the University of Warwick. I knew I wanted to do something involving engineering and maths, so this felt like the right choice for me. "I had to really focus over the last year and now I've got where I wanted to be." Rosmary Joshy achieved two Distinction* grades and one Distinction across her Level 3 vocational subjects, including top grades in digital media and ICT. She said: "I was very excited and really pleased with my results. It still feels unbelievable to me, so I'm very happy. "I'm going to apply for apprenticeships in digital marketing or IT. I've always been good with technology and I'm creative as well, so I thought I could combine both of those interests. "The first year was tough for me and I experienced some mental health challenges while changing my subjects and trying to find the right path. I followed my gut feeling about what was right for me." Natalia Pilc achieved A, A*, A*, A* in psychology, history, English and Polish. She said: "I'm shocked and still shaking. I can't believe it. I didn't expect to do this well, particularly in history, so I'm incredibly happy. "I'm now going to study law at the University of Warwick. I hope to become a solicitor specialising in either criminal or corporate law. The fact that I've come through with these results makes me really proud." Isaac Onuwuka achieved A*, A*, A in mathematics, physics and chemistry. He said: "I'm really excited to get my results. Physics was probably the most difficult subject, but I've always loved science, so I'm really pleased. "I'm now going to take a gap year to work before applying to study electrical engineering. I would eventually like to work in prosthetics, as my mum works in a hospital and that has inspired me to pursue a career where I can help and support people." Bartosz Okuniewski achieved Distinction*, Distinction, Distinction in ICT, digital media and business. He said: "I've done better than I expected. I'm now hoping to secure an apprenticeship in administration or human resources. I'm passionate about learning, which is why I think an apprenticeship is the right route for me. "I want to find a job with good career opportunities and somewhere I can stay for a long time. It's important to choose subjects you enjoy because then that knowledge stays with you." Eden Pollock achieved Distinction, C, Distinction in health and social care, psychology and applied science. She said: "I was in shock initially because I've worked so hard for this. "I'm now going to Coventry University to study adult nursing. I've always been inspired to help people and I'm looking forward to being able to do that for patients and service users. "Each of my subjects has helped me to develop the knowledge and understanding I will need for my future career. All the hard work was worth it and I'm grateful to everyone who helped me." Laura Burtonwood, Principal at Cardinal Wiseman Catholic School, said: "We are incredibly proud of all of our students receiving their results today. Their achievements are a reflection of the hard work, determination and resilience they have shown throughout their time at Cardinal Wiseman. "In many ways, today's successes are about something even greater than merely results. They are a culmination of the small choices made and the determination to keep going when things became difficult. "Behind every grade is a young person who has worked hard, overcome challenges and refused to give up. Today is about celebrating that journey as much as the results themselves. "These results have opened doors to an exciting future for our students. Whether they are heading to university, beginning an apprenticeship, entering employment or pursuing another pathway, we wish them every success as they begin this next chapter. "I would also like to thank our dedicated staff and the families who have supported our young people throughout their journey. Their encouragement, belief and hard work have played an important part in helping our students achieve their goals." Bishop Challoner Catholic School - Birmingham Bishop Challoner Catholic School Sixth Form reports another fantastic year of post-16 success. Executive Headteacher Adam Hall said: "These results are a wonderful celebration of everything our students have achieved. At Bishop Challoner we believe in 'doing ordinary things extraordinarily well', and this year group has embodied that philosophy through their everyday commitment, perseverance and ambition. We are immensely proud of every one of them." Head of School, Ranjit Pabila, added, " We are incredibly proud of our students and their achievements this summer. These results are a testament to their hard work, resilience and ambition, as well as the outstanding commitment of our staff. Achieving ALPS 2 for A Levels places us in the top 10% nationally, while our ALPS 1 rating for BTEC places our vocational provision in the top 1% nationally. These are exceptional achievements and demonstrate the breadth and quality of education we provide. We are delighted to celebrate with our students today and wish every one of them the very best as they progress to university, higher and degree-level apprenticeships, employment and the next stage of their education and careers." Results were strong across the board, however standout results were posted by the Biology Department, with 100% achieving A*-A grades, the Chemistry Department, with 80% achieving A*-B grades, and the Sociology Department, with 92% achieving A*-B grades. Vocational subjects also performed exceptionally well, with an impressive 92% of students attaining D*D*D*-DDD grades in Btec Business. Vocational subjects also performed exceptionally well, with an impressive 90% of students attaining D*D*D*-DDD grades in Btec Health and Social Care. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images Russia Revealed: how Russia uses mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizens Research shows tens of millions of people are being forced to use platform that amounts to ‘backdoor’ on their device Aisha Down and Pjotr Sauer Fri 18 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max. Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app. It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max. Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls. But while WeChat was developed over decades, in step with China’s other internet controls, Max has been imposed on a population that once had mostly-free internet access. View image in fullscreen Max is described as ‘a blueprint any government can follow’ towards digital authoritarianism. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images Now, forensic research has revealed a fuller picture of Max’s powerful surveillance capabilities . These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan. “We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens. Max is “a blueprint any government can follow” towards digital authoritarianism, said Ensafi. It represents the cutting edge of what governments such as Iran, Kazakhstan and India may soon try to achieve. Ensafi’s team were able to download the version of the app used in Russia. They found that Max can screenshot users’ devices – and the contents of its mini-apps – without their knowledge. It can access all the information stored in these mini-apps, their messages and payments. It can impersonate its users without them knowing. It can even inject code into mini-apps – which would mean, said Ensafi, that the Russian government could use Max to launch cyberattacks. Their research adds new clarity into an ongoing debate on Max’s surveillance capabilities. Crucially, said Ensafi, it cannot break into apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, if users have these installed. However, Russia has banned both. Many Russians working in or around state institutions have in effect been forced to use Max. Officials and public-sector employees, university students, teachers and even schoolchildren have all faced pressure to move their communications on to the platform. One schoolteacher in Moscow said staff at their school were ordered to switch to Max after instructions from the city authorities. “The school director called us in last March and told us directly: from now on, everything is on Max. That included chats with parents, sending out homework and other school communication,” the teacher said. “There isn’t really an option to say no, so in the end you just use the app,” they added. View image in fullscreen The Russian State Duma deputy, Sergey Boyarsky, demonstrating an age verification system using the Max app at a supermarket in February. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images Daniil, a university student in St Petersburg, said he reluctantly downloaded Max shortly before the start of the academic year after being told students would be denied access to university buildings or dormitories without a QR code generated through the app. He said he had concerns about the app’s security and privacy, but felt he had little choice if he wanted to continue accessing campus. Among Russia’s elite, use of Max often appears to be largely performative, with Telegram and Signal still widely used for day-to-day communication, according to several well-connected figures and prominent businesspeople. One person in the Kremlin’s inner circle said he and several friends had bought second phones solely to install Max, while continuing to use their main devices and preferred messaging apps as before. “It’s all for show. No one in politics really uses it,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Max has yet to replace Telegram as a major source of news for Russians. Public channels – used by media outlets, bloggers and officials to broadcast news and commentary to large audiences – remain far less developed on Max, where only a small number have built audiences comparable to the biggest channels on Telegram. Several Max users contacted by the Guardian said the app closely resembles Telegram, long Russia’s most popular messaging platform, in its design and functionality, but concerns about privacy and surveillance were widespread. “Using Max feels like you never quite know who else might be watching,” said Nikolai, a 34-year-old consultant in Moscow. While the app looked modern and slick, Nikolai said there was always something slightly sinister about using it. “You end up using it more and more because the alternatives are becoming harder to access. But it still doesn’t feel right.” Russia’s success in rapidly pushing out Max should be a “wake-up call”, said Ensafi. China reached its current state of digital authoritarianism over the course of 35 years. But Russia has imposed these sweeping restrictions – shepherding people on to a state-controlled internet – in just a decade. “The world is changing, the infrastructure of private communication is changing – and the assault by authoritarian governments is very aggressive,” she said. Max and VKontakte were approached for comment.
